name: AI compute: NVIDIA's supply chain
thesis: NVIDIA is still growing faster than its suppliers can add capacity: Q2 FY27 revenue was $96.2B (+106% y/y) with a $108B Q3 guide, and the Big 4 hyperscalers plan roughly $725B+ of 2026 capex with 2027 modeled above $1T. The money that flows through NVIDIA is now being captured by whoever owns the scarcest input, which in late 2026 is HBM and DRAM, CoWoS and substrates (ABF film, T-glass), lasers and fiber, and above all electric power (gas turbines, transformers, switchgear). The best risk/reward picks and shovels are chokepoint suppliers with pricing power and multiyear contracts (SK hynix, Micron, TSMC, ASML, Advantest, Amphenol, Credo, Lumentum, Corning, GE Vernova, Vertiv) rather than thin-margin assemblers. The Rubin transition (100% liquid cooled, HBM4, M9 boards, 1.6T optics) and Kyber (600 kW racks on 800V DC) raise content per rack for cooling, power, optics and boards, but Rubin's mainstream ramp may slip into 2027 on HBM. The main threats are a capex pause, custom ASICs (TPU, Trainium) taking share, and Taiwan concentration.

name: AI power and the grid
thesis: AI data centers have turned flat US power demand into a growth market, and the binding constraint is now physical equipment, not chips: gas turbines are sold out for years, large transformers take three to four years, and PJM capacity auctions are clearing at the price cap. The best risk/reward sits with suppliers of scarce long lead hardware (turbines, transformers, switchgear, HV cable, grain oriented steel) and with owners of existing firm generation (nuclear and gas) that can sign long term contracts with hyperscalers. Speed to power is creating a parallel behind the meter market (fuel cells, aeroderivative and reciprocating engines, batteries) that bypasses slow grid interconnection. Nuclear is a slower, policy backed second wave (Westinghouse AP1000 program, SMRs, HALEU enrichment) where fuel supply is the chokepoint. The main risk is an AI capex pause that strands orders placed at peak lead times.

Off grid gas keeps winning because the grid queue is too slow.

name: Critical materials and geopolitics
thesis: China's export controls on rare earths, gallium, germanium, antimony and graphite turned critical materials from a commodity trade into a national security trade, and the US government responded by becoming an equity owner, offtaker and price floor provider (MP Materials, Lithium Americas, Trilogy Metals, Vulcan Elements, Korea Zinc, Intel). Policy now underwrites the downside for selected Western producers, which changes the risk profile for long term holders and makes these names more attractive for put selling than their volatile history suggests. The near term swing factor is the expiry of China's suspensions. The October 2025 rare earth rules were due back on November 10, 2026, but the US China truce was extended to January 10, 2027 (Bessent on Sep 23, China's commerce ministry on Sep 28). The gallium, germanium and antimony ban suspension is dated November 27, 2026, and no source yet confirms it moved too. Copper is the large cap anchor: grid and data center demand plus the Grasberg disruption pushed prices to records in 2026.

name: Defense, drones and reshoring
thesis: Western defense spending is in a multi year step up: the US FY2027 request is $1.5 trillion including $350 billion via reconciliation, and NATO allies committed to 5% of GDP by 2035 (3.5% core). The 2025 to 2026 conflicts burned interceptors faster than production lines could replace them, so the money is flowing first to munitions, missile defense, solid rocket motors and cheap mass (drones and counter drone). The constraint is industrial capacity, not budgets, which favors suppliers of chokepoint components (rocket motors, seekers, energetics, shipyard capacity) and the contractors building new plants. Reshoring of chips and defense production adds a parallel construction and automation wave, though CHIPS fab timelines have slipped. The government is also becoming an owner (Intel 9.9%, L3Harris Missile Solutions preferred), which reduces downside for chosen champions but adds policy risk.

name: Fintech and Crypto Rails: Stablecoins, Tokenization, Exchanges
thesis: The GENIUS Act (signed July 18, 2025) made dollar stablecoins a regulated payment instrument backed by cash and short Treasuries, so stablecoin issuers are now large, rate sensitive buyers of T-bills, and banks, card networks and fintechs have a legal path to issue or settle in tokens. Implementation is arriving in 2026: Treasury's first interim final rule (Sep 30, 2026) set a $10 billion line above which issuers cannot use state regulation, and the OCC has said it will finalize its rule by November 2026. The broader market structure bill (CLARITY) failed a Senate cloture vote 49 to 50 on Sep 15, 2026, so exchange and token rules stay with the agencies for now. The money flows to whoever controls distribution and reserves (Tether, Circle and its distributor Coinbase), to incumbents that bought or built stablecoin rails (Mastercard closed BVNK, Visa settles in USDC), and to custodians. Higher for longer short rates help issuers. The losers are high fee rails (remittances still average 6.36% to send $200) and, more slowly, card interchange. Bitcoin treasury companies are a leveraged, reflexive side bet whose premiums can collapse when bitcoin stalls.
money_source: Stablecoin issuers earn interest on reserves (mostly T-bills and repo), so revenue scales with float times short rates. DefiLlama showed about $312 billion of dollar stablecoins on Oct 5, 2026, with USDT about $184 billion and USDC about $74 billion. Circle earned $668 million of reserve income in Q2 2026, 95% of its $701 million revenue. The Fed raised rates to 3.75% to 4.00% on Sep 16, 2026, which lifts reserve income. Bitcoin treasury companies are the other big inflow: Strategy held 848,000 BTC as of Oct 4, 2026, bought at an average of about $75,441. Banks and payment companies are spending on tokenized deposits and stablecoin settlement: JPMorgan's JPMD runs on Base, Visa's stablecoin settlement passed a $20 billion annualized run rate (September 2026), and Mastercard paid up to $1.8 billion for BVNK (closed Aug 3, 2026).

name: GLP-1 and obesity
thesis: Obesity drugs are moving from a supply constrained, high price injectable market to a mass market of cheaper pills and government covered access, so volume is exploding while price per patient falls. Lilly has pulled ahead of Novo on efficacy, supply and the oral launch, and its tirzepatide franchise is now the largest drug franchise in the world by quarterly sales. The 2026 policy turn (TrumpRx pricing, $50 Medicare copay via the GLP-1 Bridge starting July 2026, and the $274 negotiated Medicare semaglutide price in 2027) trades margin for volume. Picks and shovels shift as the mix moves to pills: peptide and small molecule API capacity, CDMOs and devices still grow, but the next leg of volume growth favors API and tablet capacity over pens. Second order effects on food, medtech, diagnostics and insurers are real but slower than headlines suggest.

name: Healthcare and Medtech: Aging, Heart, Sugar, Hearing, Sight
thesis: The single biggest payer in the world, Medicare, is growing faster than the rest of US health spending because 70 million plus people are enrolled and the 75 to 84 cohort is swelling. That money flows disproportionately to procedures and devices that treat age-related disease: aortic stenosis, atrial fibrillation, diabetes, hearing loss, cataract and retinal disease. The durable winners are platform owners with clinical data moats and reimbursement codes (da Vinci, CGM, anti-VEGF, structural heart) and the consumable and component suppliers that every platform needs. 2026 has shown the cracks too: Watchman and pulsed field ablation competition cut Boston Scientific guidance twice, Integer cut guidance on customer adoption misses and is now being taken private, and tariff and drug pricing policy is a live wildcard.
money_source: US national health expenditures were about $5.7 trillion in 2025 (18.4% of GDP) and are projected at $6.0 trillion in 2026 and $9.0 trillion by 2034 (CMS Office of the Actuary). Medicare spending growth is projected to accelerate from 7.7% in 2025 to 9.2% in 2026, the fastest of the major payers. Medicare enrollment passed 70 million in early 2026 (70.3 million in April 2026 CMS data), with Medicare Advantage above 51% of enrollees. Hospitals and Medicare Advantage plans are therefore the main buyers of devices; consumers are now a second buyer in hearing (OTC and AirPods) and myopia lenses.

name: Robotics, Automation and Physical AI
thesis: Physical AI is moving from demos to early production: Tesla is pouring a record $25 billion plus into 2026 capex across AI, Optimus and robotaxi, Hyundai plans a 30,000 per year Atlas factory, and Waymo is doubling paid rides. Humanoid volumes are still tiny (about 18,000 units globally in 2025 per IDC), so the reliable money today is in the parts every robot needs: precision reducers, bearings, frameless motors, rare earth magnets, vision sensors and AI compute. China already leads humanoid shipments and controls most rare earth magnet supply, which makes magnets and reducers the true chokepoints. Expect most humanoid makers to disappoint on timelines while component suppliers, compute and warehouse automation earn real revenue.
money_source: Tesla raised 2026 capex guidance to more than $25 billion (vs $8.5 billion spent in 2025), for AI training, chips, Optimus manufacturing capacity and robotaxi, and expects negative free cash flow for the rest of 2026. Figure AI raised over $1 billion at a $39 billion valuation (Sept 2025); humanoid startups raised $3.2 billion globally in 2025. Hyundai plans a factory for 30,000 Atlas robots per year by 2028. Waymo (Alphabet) is funding a push from about 500,000 to 1 million paid rides per week by end of 2026. The US Department of Defense took an equity stake in MP Materials with a 10 year $110 per kg NdPr price floor (July 2025). Symbotic holds a $22.5 billion backlog, mostly Walmart.

name: Space, Quantum and Cyber: Government Funded Frontier Tech
thesis: The common money source is government: the Pentagon (Golden Dome missile defense, Space Development Agency constellations), the Commerce Department and DARPA for quantum, and every enterprise and agency for cybersecurity. In space, SpaceX is the launch chokepoint and is now public (SPCX, listed June 12, 2026), worth about $2.26T at the Oct 5, 2026 close, so the rest of the group is priced against it. The investable picks around it are suppliers, satellite builders, defense primes and the few credible launch challengers. Quantum is real science and revenue is finally growing fast at IonQ, but the pure plays still trade at high multiples of small sales and keep raising money, now partly from the government in exchange for equity. Treat them as option premium sources, not compounders. Cybersecurity is the most proven cash generator of the three, and the big consolidation deals (Palo Alto with CyberArk closed; Google with Wiz cleared the EU) are done or nearly done.
money_source: Golden Dome: the administration put the cost at about $185B, but CBO estimated on May 12, 2026 that a Golden Dome style shield could cost about $1.2T over 20 years, with space based interceptors the biggest piece (about $448B without them). Congress has provided roughly $25B through the 2025 reconciliation law and about $13.4B in fiscal 2026 appropriations. Space Systems Command awarded 20 contracts worth up to $3.2B to 12 companies (including LMT, NOC, RTX and SpaceX) to prototype space based interceptors (May 2026). SDA Tranche 3 Tracking Layer awards in December 2025 totaled about $3.5B (Lockheed about $1.1B, L3Harris about $843M, Rocket Lab $816M, Northrop about $764M). SpaceX: IPO June 12, 2026; Google agreed to pay SpaceX $920M a month for AI compute at its xAI data centers from October 2026 to June 2029. EchoStar's spectrum sales to SpaceX total about $19.6B, with up to about $11.1B paid in SpaceX stock. Quantum: the Commerce Department is giving more than $2B in CHIPS Act money to nine quantum firms in exchange for minority stakes, including $100M each to D-Wave, Rigetti and Quantinuum (D-Wave's final agreement signed Sep 8, 2026). Cyber: Palo Alto closed its about $25B CyberArk deal on Feb 11, 2026, and Google's $32B Wiz deal won EU approval a day later.
